title: Stop agents colliding on a bead someone already claimed
description:
## Summary

Two agents keep starting work on the same bead. The cause is not carelessness — it is that a claim
looks abandoned within minutes of being taken.

`bd update <id> --claim` takes a **lease** with a short TTL, kept alive only by `bd heartbeat`.
Neither `CLAUDE.md` nor the `beads-workflow` skill mentions `bd heartbeat` at all, so no agent here
has ever sent one. A work cycle in this repo — RED, GREEN, REFACTOR, a full local gate, CI — runs an
hour or more against a TTL of roughly five minutes.

Observed, on a bead an agent had claimed ten minutes earlier and was demonstrably still working
(it had already wired a dependency from it):

```
◐ ah-xde · Remove the Classic map theme   [P2 · IN_PROGRESS]
Lease: expires in 1 min (heartbeat 3 mins ago)
```

`bd reclaim` is the reaper: it finds in_progress issues whose lease expired, **clears the assignee
and sets them back to open** so another worker can claim them. `bd update --force` documents itself
as being for "abandoned claims — crashed agent, expired lease". With nobody heartbeating, every live
claim in this repository matches that description exactly.

Three contributing findings:

- **The selection window.** The loop claims before branching, but exploration and planning happen
  first — one bead was planned for ten minutes before it was claimed. Selected-but-unclaimed work is
  invisible to every other agent.
- **Worktrees are not the problem.** All three worktrees resolve to the same Dolt database, so a
  claim is visible locally the moment it is written.
- **Cross-machine is.** Leases are node-local and write no Dolt commit; only status and assignee
  commit, and those travel only on `bd dolt push`/`bd dolt pull`. The skill says to push at session
  end, so a claim can stay invisible to another machine for an entire session.

`claim.ttl` is not a documented config key — `bd config get claim.ttl` reports "not set", and the
skill already records that `bd config set` accepts unknown keys silently — so lengthening the TTL is
not a reliable lever. The fix belongs in the instructions.

## Scope

Update `.claude/skills/beads-workflow/SKILL.md` and `CLAUDE.md` (the symlink to
`.github/copilot-instructions.md`) with four rules, agreed with the navigator:

1. **Claim first.** `bd update <id> --claim` is the first action after choosing a bead — before
   exploring, planning or asking questions, not merely before branching. A failed claim means
   somebody else won; pick another bead.
2. **Heartbeat while working.** `bd heartbeat <id>` at every phase gate and before any long wait (a
   full smoke run, a CI watch). Heartbeats write no Dolt commit and no history, so the cadence is
   free.
3. **Never take over a claim unasked.** `in_progress` with an assignee is authoritative whatever the
   lease says. No `bd reclaim`, no `bd update --force`, no reassignment over a live claim without
   the navigator saying so — an expired lease here means "nobody heartbeated", not "the worker
   died".
4. **Push the claim immediately.** `bd dolt push` right after claiming, not only at session end, so
   another machine can see it. Keep the session-end push as well.

Record the lease behaviour itself in the skill's Traps section, so an agent that meets a stale lease
recognises it rather than reasoning from `--force`'s help text.

## Out of scope

- Changing `claim.ttl` or any beads configuration; the key is not part of the documented surface.
- A supervisor process running `bd reclaim` on a timer. That is the upstream design for dead-worker
  recovery, and it is exactly what must not run here while nothing heartbeats.

## Validation

- `bd heartbeat <id>` on a bead this session holds, confirming the lease moves forward — the one
  claim in the four rules that has never actually been exercised here.
- Re-read both documents end to end: the daily loop, the checklist and CLAUDE.md's work-package
  rules must agree with each other, since all three currently describe claiming.
- No code changes, so the gate is `pnpm run lint` for the markdown-adjacent tooling only.
acceptance_criteria:
The beads-workflow skill and CLAUDE.md both say to claim before exploring or planning, not merely before branching.
Both say to heartbeat during long work, naming bd heartbeat.
Both forbid bd reclaim, bd update --force and reassignment over a live claim without the navigator's approval.
Both say to bd dolt push straight after claiming, in addition to at session end.
The skill's Traps section explains the lease TTL and why an expired lease here does not mean an abandoned worker.

title: Roads do not shrink with the map when zooming out
description:
## Summary

Zoomed far out, roads stop being lines and become blobs: the mark is wider than the hex it belongs
to. Reported against Miniature World and Beveled Tile, but the cause is shared and **every theme has
it** — they differ only in degree.

Each theme's `RoadLayer` draws a spoke from the hex centre along `ROAD_VECTORS[direction]`, scaled by
`HEX_RADIUS * 0.87` (0.83 in Beveled Tile). The **length** is therefore hex-relative and shrinks with
the world transform. The **width** is not: every road line carries
`vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke"`, which pins the stroke to a constant number of screen pixels at
any zoom. Nothing in any theme divides a road width by the scale or expresses it in fractions of
`HEX_RADIUS`, and the CSS road classes set colour only, never width — the JSX `strokeWidth` is the
whole story.

At `MIN_STEP = -8` the scale is 0.25 (`mapViewport.ts:35-37,78-80`), so an 18-unit hex is 4.5px on
screen and a spoke is about 3.9px long:

| theme | road stroke (constant screen px) | spoke at min zoom | width ÷ length |
|---|---|---|---|
| classic | 7 | 3.9px | ~1.8× |
| miniatureWorld | 5 | 3.9px | ~1.3× |
| beveledTile | 4 | 3.7px | ~1.1× |
| cartographersTable | 4 casing + 1.4 dash | 3.9px | ~1.0× |
| emblemAndDots | 3.4 | 3.9px | ~0.87× |
| tacticalHud | 2 | 3.9px | ~0.51× |

It reads worst at far zoom because the zoom-band CSS deliberately hides labels, pips, chips and
glyphs there while **keeping** roads (each theme.css says so — e.g. beveledTile "far keeps the tile,
its bevel and the roads"). So the fattest thing on screen is the only thing left on screen.

## Scope

- The six `RoadLayer` functions: `classic/index.tsx:58`, `cartographersTable/index.tsx:168`,
  `beveledTile/index.tsx:179`, `emblemAndDots/index.tsx:137`, `tacticalHud/index.tsx:159`,
  `miniatureWorld/index.tsx:216`.
- Agreed target: **a road keeps its proportion to the hex at every zoom.** In this codebase that
  means dropping `vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke"` from the road marks and expressing the width in
  fractions of `HEX_RADIUS`, which is the rule `mapThemes/geometry.ts:4-6` already states for marks:
  "in fractions of HEX_RADIUS rather than in absolute pixels". Each theme keeps its own relative
  weight — Tactical HUD's road stays the thinnest, Miniature World's the heaviest.
- Regression test modelled on the one that already pins the opposite behaviour for the fog lattice,
  `tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts:2011` ("the unexplored lattice keeps a constant hairline at every
  zoom"). That test asserts computed `stroke-width × --map-scale === 1` screen pixel. A road wants
  the mirror of it: computed `stroke-width` constant in **user** units across zoom steps, so its
  screen width falls with the scale. Assert it at rest, zoomed in, and at `MIN_STEP`.
- No theme currently has any test asserting a road's width or its scaling — the road tests only
  count lines and check for dashes. Whatever shape the fix takes, that gap is what let this ship.

## Two things the fix has to decide, not assume

1. **Does a road still read at far zoom once it shrinks?** The far band keeps roads precisely
   because they are the last legible structure. A width that is a true fraction of the hex is about
   1px on screen at `MIN_STEP`. If that turns out to be too faint, the honest answer is a floor
   expressed against the hex (never wider than some share of it) rather than a return to a constant
   screen width. Look at it before choosing.
2. **The route overlay is also non-scaling** (`MapCanvas.tsx:736,744` — a 5px casing and a 3px line),
   and Classic's road width of 7 was tuned explicitly against it, per the comment at
   `classic/index.tsx:52-57`: wide enough that "whether a path runs along a road or misses it stays
   legible at every zoom". If roads scale and the route overlay does not, that relationship inverts
   somewhere in the zoom range. Decide whether the overlay follows the roads.

## Out of scope

- Labels, pips, chips and the fog hairline, which are constant-screen-size deliberately and have
  their own zoom-band rules.
- Any change to road *placement* or to which hexes report roads.
- Classic, if `ah-xde` (removing that theme) has landed first — it is the worst offender at 7px, so
  the order of these two beads decides whether it is worth touching.

## Validation

- `pnpm test` — the theme road tests, plus whatever unit-level assertion the fix adds.
- `pnpm test:smoke` — both shells, including the new road-scaling test.
- `pnpm check` before the PR.
- By hand, and this is the part that actually answers it: open a hex with roads in Miniature World
  and Beveled Tile, zoom to `MIN_STEP`, and confirm a road reads as a line within its hex rather
  than a blob across it — then zoom to `MAX_STEP` and confirm it has not become a slab.
design: Target agreed with the navigator: a road keeps its proportion to the hex at every zoom. The cause is vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke" on every road line, which pins the width to screen pixels while the spoke length stays hex-relative - so the two diverge as the map scales. Reported for Miniature World and Beveled Tile; investigation found all six themes affected, Classic worst at 7px against a 3.9px spoke at minimum zoom. Two questions are left open on purpose because they need to be looked at rather than reasoned about: whether a proportional road still reads at far zoom, where the zoom band keeps roads as the last visible structure, and whether the route overlay - also non-scaling, and what Classic's width was tuned against - should follow the roads.
acceptance_criteria:
At MIN_STEP a road reads as a line inside its hex rather than a mark wider than the hex, in every theme that ships.
A road's width is expressed against HEX_RADIUS rather than in constant screen pixels, so its on-screen width falls with the map scale.
A smoke test pins the scaling across zoom steps, mirroring the fog lattice's constant-hairline test rather than repeating it.
Each theme keeps its own relative road weight - the thin ones stay thin, the heavy ones stay heavy.
pnpm check passes.

title: Remove the Classic map theme
description:
## Summary

Remove the **Classic** map theme. It is the map as it looked before the five designed themes
arrived, and it is now the least of them; keeping it costs a directory of drawing code, a share of
every theme-wide change, and a slot in the settings picker.

Classic is not an ordinary registry entry, which is what makes this more than a deletion. It is
**`DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID`**, and it is the hard-coded last resort inside `getMapTheme` for a registry
that contains no default at all. Both have to move before the directory can go.

**Cartographer's Table becomes the new default** (decided with the navigator).

## Scope

- Delete `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/classic/` — `index.tsx` and `classic.test.tsx`.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/index.ts`: drop the import and the `MAP_THEMES` entry,
  point `DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID` at `cartographers-table`, and replace the `?? classic` last resort in
  `getMapTheme` with the new default's module. Update the file header comment, which currently
  describes the order as "the map as it was, then the five designs".
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/index.test.tsx` — the registry tests name Classic
  directly, including the fallback-of-last-resort case.
- Persisted settings need no migration code: `knownMapTheme` in
  `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts:142` already answers `DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID` for any id the
  registry does not know, so a stored `"classic"` moves to the new default on the next load. This is
  worth an explicit test rather than an assumption — a stored `"classic"` must land on
  Cartographer's Table, not throw and not render nothing.
- `tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts` — five assertions name `classic` or `map-theme-classic`, including
  the picker's default value and a test that switches away from Classic and back to it. They need
  rewriting around two themes that still ship.
- Docs, rewritten against the new default rather than merely struck: `docs/ui/hex-rendering.md`
  describes what is drawn largely in terms of what Classic draws (its opening note, the "not yet
  implemented" list at the foot); `docs/ui/README.md` says "All six ship: Classic, plus the five
  designs" and carries a Classic Commander layout section; `docs/ui/map-themes.md` is the registry's
  own reference.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/hexView.ts:53` mentions "the classic hull names" — that
  is Atlantis ship vocabulary, not the theme. Leave it.

## Out of scope

- Any change to the other five themes' drawing.
- A migration dialog or a notice telling the user their theme changed. The silent fallback is the
  agreed behaviour.

## Validation

- `pnpm test` — registry tests, the new stored-`"classic"` fallback test, settings store tests.
- `pnpm test:smoke` — both shells; the map theme picker walk is the one that moves most.
- `pnpm check` before the PR.
- By hand: open the app with `"classic"` already in `atlantis-hud-settings`, confirm the map draws
  as Cartographer's Table and the picker shows it, and confirm the picker no longer offers Classic.
design: Cartographer's Table becomes the new default, chosen with the navigator as the most map-like of the remaining five and the next in registry order. No migration code is written: knownMapTheme already answers DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID for an unknown id, so a stored "classic" moves across on the next load - the point is to test that rather than assume it. Docs are rewritten in the same bead rather than split off, because hex-rendering.md describes the map in terms of what Classic draws and would otherwise document a theme that no longer exists.
acceptance_criteria:
The settings picker no longer offers Classic, and packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/classic/ is gone.
DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID is cartographers-table, and getMapTheme's last resort for a registry without a default no longer mentions Classic.
A settings blob holding mapTheme "classic" loads as Cartographer's Table rather than failing or drawing nothing, pinned by a test.
docs/ui/hex-rendering.md, docs/ui/README.md and docs/ui/map-themes.md describe the themes that actually ship, with the rendering prose rewritten against the new default.
pnpm check passes.

title: Refresh the beads issues export at pre-push instead of on every commit
description:
`.beads/issues.jsonl` is a generated file that is committed so the backlog is diffable in the repo.
Keeping it fresh is currently an obligation on every commit: `export.auto: true` in
`.beads/config.yaml` makes the bd pre-commit hook write it, and the beads-workflow skill's
end-of-session checklist asks for `bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl` by hand. Auto-export is
throttled to once a minute, and it has already committed a snapshot that still held a bead deleted
minutes earlier (#132 documented the trap and the `git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l` check
that catches it). Two sessions in a row have then ended with the export knowingly out of date,
because refreshing it means a commit straight to `main`.

Move the obligation to push time, where it is needed once per branch instead of once per commit and
where nothing can be pushed stale.

## Scope

- A repo-owned gate that runs from `.beads/hooks/pre-push`, below the `BEADS INTEGRATION` markers
  so `bd hooks install` preserves it (`bd hooks install --help`: user content outside the markers
  survives installs and upgrades).
- The gate exports the database to a temporary file and compares it with the committed
  `.beads/issues.jsonl`. Equal: the push proceeds and the gate says nothing. Different: the gate
  writes the fresh export, commits that one file as `chore(beads): refresh the issues export`, and
  aborts the push with a message saying the commit was made and to push again.
- A pre-push hook cannot amend or extend the commits being pushed — the refs are already computed —
  so the refresh is a new commit and the push is aborted rather than rewritten. No `--force` is
  ever needed.
- `export.auto` goes to `false`, which is beads' own default, so no throttled snapshot can reach a
  commit again.
- The gate is inert when it cannot do its job: no `bd` on PATH, no `.beads` directory, or a
  `bd export` that fails must let the push through rather than block it. A tooling convenience must
  not stand between the player and their remote.
- The beads-workflow skill loses the per-session export step and gains a short description of the
  gate, replacing the trap section's manual verification advice.
- Repo tooling has no test home today, so the gate's decision logic is written to be unit-testable
  and a root vitest project is wired up for `scripts/`, run by `pnpm run check` and by the CI
  `checks` job.

## Out of scope

- Whether the export is committed at all — that question was settled in favour of keeping it.
- The Dolt remote and `bd dolt push`, which stay exactly as they are.
- The other four bd hooks.
- Any CI check that validates the export server-side.

## Validation

- Unit tests for the gate: unchanged export, changed export, missing `.beads`, absent `bd`, and a
  failing `bd export`.
- An end-to-end shell exercise in a throwaway git repo with a bare remote and a stubbed `bd` on
  PATH: a stale export aborts the first push with the refresh commit in place, and the second push
  succeeds with the fresh file in it.
- `pnpm run check` and the CI gate.
- Manually, on this branch: with a deliberately stale JSONL, `git push` refuses once, leaves the
  refresh commit, and succeeds on the retry.
acceptance_criteria:
A repo-owned gate runs from .beads/hooks/pre-push, below the beads markers, and survives bd hooks install.
A push whose committed .beads/issues.jsonl matches a fresh bd export proceeds silently.
A push whose committed export is stale is aborted, with the fresh export committed alone as chore(beads): refresh the issues export, and the retry succeeds.
No push is ever rewritten or needs --force.
export.auto is false in .beads/config.yaml.
The gate lets the push through when bd is absent, .beads is missing, or bd export fails.
The beads-workflow skill drops the per-session export step and describes the gate instead.
The gate's logic is covered by unit tests that run in pnpm run check and in CI.

title: Remember map zoom level and focus hex across reloads
description:
The map view resets when a game is reloaded. The user has to zoom and pan back to where they were working.

Goal: persist the map viewport per game so reloading restores the previous view.

Scope:
- Persist current zoom level and the focused/centered hex
- Restore them when the same game is loaded again
- Fall back to the current default view when no saved state exists (e.g. first load of a game)

Acceptance criteria:
- Reloading a game restores the zoom level and centered hex from the previous session
- Viewport state is stored per game, so switching between games does not mix up views

title: Map forgets known-but-never-occupied hexes once no unit can see them
description:
When a unit moves away, the map stops showing hexes that were known only from that unit's line of sight. Only the hex the unit itself occupied earlier remains on the map; the surrounding 6 hexes (e.g. ocean hexes seen from a fleet jump but never entered) disappear.

Expected: once a hex has been observed in any report, it stays on the map as known terrain (with the data from the last turn it was observed), even when no unit can currently see it.

Actual: only hexes a unit actually occupied are remembered; adjacent observed-only hexes are dropped when they leave current visibility.

Acceptance criteria:
- Hexes observed from an adjacent unit remain visible on the map after the unit leaves
- Remembered hexes show the terrain and data from the most recent turn they were observed
- Currently visible vs remembered hexes remain distinguishable (see ah-rgp)

title: Option to keep the long order format when exporting orders
description:
Exported orders come out in the short format only. The server's own unit description — name,
flags, weight, capacity, skills and what the unit can study, wrapped over as many `;` lines as it
takes — is dropped the moment a report's template becomes an editable document
(`stripUnitComments` in `packages/shared/src/ordersDocument.ts`, called once from
`documentFor` in `packages/shared/src/orderDraft.ts:113`), and `exportOrders`
(`packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx:1526`) writes that stripped document straight out.

Dropping the descriptions from the editor was deliberate (#37): the unit panel already says all of
it, and on a unit with no orders yet the description is the whole block. But the exported file is
read elsewhere — kept as a record of the turn, diffed against the next one, or read by a human
without this application in front of them — and there the long format is what makes a bare
`unit 793` legible:

```
unit 793
;Three of Five (793), behind, revealing faction, leader [LEAD]. Weight:
;  10. Capacity: 0/0/15/0. Skills: observation [OBSE] 1 (35), force
;  [FORC] 1 (35), pattern [PATT] 1 (30), spirit [SPIR] 1 (30), gate
;  lore [GATE] 1 (30), fire [FIRE] 1 (30), combat [COMB] 3 (180). Can
;  Study: earthquake [EQUA], force shield [FSHI], energy shield [ESHI],
;  spirit shield [SSHI], magical healing [MHEA], farsight [FARS], mind
;  reading [MIND], weather lore [WEAT], earth lore [EART], necromancy
;  [NECR], demon lore [DEMO], illusion [ILLU], artifact lore [ARTI].
@study obse
```

So the option belongs on the export, not on the editor: the descriptions stay out of the panel the
player writes in, and go back into the file on the way out when asked for.

## Scope

- An option on the orders export that puts the server's long-format unit descriptions back into the
  exported text. Default off, so today's output is unchanged unless the player asks.
- The descriptions are recovered from the report's own template (`parsed.ordersTemplate`), matched
  per `unit` block, rather than kept in the document — the document must stay as it is, or the
  editor regains the clutter #37 removed.
- Each unit's description is written directly under its `unit` line, above the player's orders, in
  the server's own wrapping, byte for byte as the report carried it.
- Units the template has no description for (a unit formed this turn by the player) simply get
  none; the export must not fail or invent one.
- The player's own `;` notes in the draft are untouched and not duplicated.
- The same option and the same output on both shells — web download and desktop save alike.

## Out of scope

- Any change to what the editor shows, or to `stripUnitComments` at seed time.
- The `Orders Template (Long Format):` banner and the region `;*** ... ***` banners — this is about
  unit descriptions only.
- The map export in `crates/core/src/report/export.rs`, which is a separate path.
- Reformatting or re-wrapping descriptions; they go out as they came in.

## Validation

- `pnpm run check` and `cargo test` (or `pnpm run check` alone if the change stays in TypeScript).
- A unit test over the committed turn 71 fixture: export with the option on, and every `unit` line
  that has a description in the template is followed by exactly those `;` lines, in that order.
- The same export with the option off is byte for byte what is exported today.
- Round trip: an export written with the option on, imported back as a draft, seeds a document with
  the descriptions stripped again — no accumulation.
- A smoke test exercising the checkbox from the orders panel, on web and desktop-shell.
- Manually: export a turn with the option on, and read the file — a leader's eight-line description
  should be intact and correctly indented.
acceptance_criteria:
The orders export offers an option, default off, that writes the server's long-format unit descriptions into the exported file.
With the option off the exported text is byte for byte what is exported today.
With the option on, every unit whose template block carried a description has those ';' lines directly under its 'unit' line, verbatim and in order, above the player's orders.
A unit with no description in the template exports without one and without error.
The player's own ';' notes are neither dropped nor duplicated.
Re-importing an export written with the option on seeds a document with the descriptions stripped, so they do not accumulate.
The option and its output are the same on the web download and the desktop save.

title: Make terrain of undiscovered hexes more visible on the map
description:
Undiscovered (not yet explored) hexes render their terrain image so heavily whitened/faded that the terrain type is not distinguishable at a glance. There are thin differences in the image background, but they are too subtle.

Goal: make it clear at a glance what terrain an undiscovered hex has, while still keeping a clear visual distinction between discovered and undiscovered hexes.

Ideas to consider:
- Reduce the whitening/desaturation amount for undiscovered hexes
- Keep the fade but add a stronger terrain-colored tint
- Use a distinct marker (outline style, hatching, reduced opacity instead of whitening) for the discovered/undiscovered distinction instead of washing out the terrain

Acceptance criteria:
- Terrain type of an undiscovered hex is recognizable at a glance in all map themes
- Discovered vs undiscovered hexes remain visually distinguishable

title: Max number of units settable from the units-in-hex pane
description:
It should be possible to increase/decrease the number of units that are shown in the units-in-hex pane by clicking a + or - located to the right on the top bar of the pane. There shall also be a text indicating what the max units shown are, as this may be more than the hex currently has.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The units-in-hex pane's top bar carries + and - controls on its right-hand side.
- Clicking + or - raises or lowers the maximum number of units listed, and the list updates immediately.
- The top bar shows the current maximum, including when the hex holds fewer units than that.
- The chosen maximum survives a reload.

title: Toggle badges on/off in the map display
description:
It should be possible to toggle different badges on/off in the map display to reduce cluttering.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each kind of badge drawn on the map can be turned on and off independently.
- The map redraws immediately when a badge kind is toggled.
- The chosen set of visible badges survives a reload.
notes: PR #138 open. desktop-shell smoke not run: port 4174 held by the navigator's tauri dev server; needs one local rerun before merge.

title: Commit a second turn so multi-step routes can be proved on real data
description:
## Summary

Commit a second real turn for one faction, so that routes longer than one step can be proved against
real data rather than only against synthetic corridors.

## Problem

Issue #8 built a map that accumulates across turns, and it works: the core merges remembered regions
with the current report, the current turn wins where they disagree, and both platforms store and
read back region sightings. All of that is unit-tested.

None of it can be demonstrated end to end, because the repository holds exactly one report per
faction: neworigins-3.0.0-f73-t2.rep for faction 73 and neworigins-3.0.0-f95-t71.rep for faction 95.

A single report cannot support a route longer than one step. It describes the hexes the faction
stood in and names their neighbours, but a named hex describes no exits of its own, so the graph
stops at the fringe. With the committed fixtures, every route the planner produces is one step.

Multi-step, multi-month, road and flight behaviour is therefore covered only against small synthetic
reports built in the tests. Those are honest tests, but they are our own fixtures rather than the
game's output, and they cannot catch a disagreement between what we think a report says and what one
actually says.

Fabricating a second turn was deliberately avoided during #8: inventing game data and committing it
as a fixture would make every test built on it worthless as evidence.

## Scope

- Commit a genuine second turn for faction 95, ideally adjacent in time to turn 71
- Add an acceptance test that imports both turns and plans a route crossing ground the later report
  does not describe
- Extend the smoke suite so the multi-step case is exercised in a browser, not only in the core

## Acceptance criteria

- Two turns of one faction are committed under tests/fixtures/reports
- A test plans a route of more than one step over the accumulated map, with a cost read from the
  reports by hand
- The stale map state is exercised, since it becomes reachable only once a hex is remembered from an
  earlier turn than the current one

## Validation

    cargo test --workspace
    pnpm run check

## Dependencies / Links

- Main issue: #1
- Follows: #8

## Note

This one needs a human: the report has to come from a real game.

title: Turn-to-turn diffs for units, regions, and orders
description:
## Summary

Compare two imported turns of a game and see what changed: units gained/lost/moved, region changes, and how the orders differ.

## Problem

The app keeps every imported turn in storage, but the player can only ever look at the latest one. Between turns the real questions are "what changed since last month?" and "what did I order last time?" — today that means opening two report text files side by side.

## Scope

- An API to enumerate the imported turns of a game (`listImportedTurns` through core-persistence, the WASM and Tauri adapters, and the shared `CoreClient`), since today only "a known turn number" or "latest" can be loaded.
- Loading a second turn alongside the current one for comparison (the app currently holds exactly one parsed report in memory).
- A diff view for a chosen turn pair surfacing adds/removes/changes for units, regions, and orders.

## Out of scope

- Diffing more than two turns at once, or cross-game comparison.
- Changes to report parsing or order validation.

## Acceptance criteria

- The user can pick two imported turns of the current game.
- The diff view lists units added, removed, and changed between the pair.
- The diff view lists region changes between the pair.
- The diff view shows how the orders drafts differ between the pair.

## Validation

- Import two consecutive turn reports with known differences; open the diff view and verify each known difference is surfaced and nothing is falsely reported.
- Vitest coverage for the diff computation modules; a Playwright smoke walk of the diff view on both web and desktop-shell projects.

## Dependencies / Links

- Broken out of issue 9 (Productivity UX), where it was originally a scope bullet; deferred to its own deliverable.
- Storage substrate already exists: `imported_turns` table keyed by game/faction/turn in `crates/core-persistence`.

title: Load multiple reports
description:
It shall be possible to load multiple reports in one go. The application shall then look at the headers of all reports to figure out in which order the reports shall be loaded. It shall be possible to load both your own and allies reports in one go.

While we are at it, the menu option for loading orders shall be changed to "Import".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Several report files can be selected and imported in one action.
- The application reads the turn number from each report header and loads them in turn order, regardless of the order they were selected in.
- Own-faction and ally reports can be imported together in the same action.
- The menu option for loading reports reads "Import".
close_reason: Delivered in PR #133: batch import of several reports, ordered by header turn, with the load control renamed Import

title: Record beads CLI traps in the beads-workflow skill
description:
Three beads behaviours bit during the #126 migration and are not obvious from the CLI help. Record them in the beads-workflow skill so the next session does not rediscover them.

- The pre-commit auto-export can write a stale snapshot: a commit picked up a JSONL still containing a throwaway bead that had already been deleted.
- `bd config set` accepts unknown keys silently, so a mistyped key reads as success; probing also rewrote a commented-out default in `.beads/config.yaml` and stripped its trailing newline.
- The `owner` field is taken from `git config user.email` at creation and has no override; `--actor` sets `created_by` only, and `--assignee` is a separate field.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `.claude/skills/beads-workflow/SKILL.md` carries a section covering all three behaviours.
- The export trap names the verification command that catches it.

title: Plan sea movement for fleets
description:
## Summary

Plan sea movement: routes for units aboard a fleet, emitting SAIL rather than MOVE.

## Problem

The planner handles land movement only. A unit standing in an ocean hex - which is what a unit
aboard a fleet looks like in a report - is refused with "the sea is in the way", and so is any
destination across water. That is correct for what #8 built, and useless for a faction that sails.

The rules make sailing a second system rather than a variation:

- A fleet has its own speed, stated per ship on the data page: a Longship moves 4 hexes per month, a
  Raft 2, a Galleon 4
- "For a fleet to enter any region only costs one movement point", so the terrain premium that
  applies to riding and walking units does not apply at sea
- Sailing needs a total of N levels of sailing skill among the crew, stated per ship
- A fleet has a cargo capacity, which the scraper already records as cargoCapacity
- Guards behave differently: a fleet enters a guarded region and is then stopped, where a land unit
  is prevented from entering at all

## Scope

- A Sail movement mode, with speed taken from the ship rather than from the unit
- Flat terrain cost at sea, per the quoted rule
- Recognising that a unit is aboard a fleet it can actually sail, including the skill requirement
- Emitting SAIL orders rather than MOVE
- Refusing a sea route with a named reason when the crew cannot sail the ship

## Out of scope

- Combat at sea
- Building or repairing ships

## Acceptance criteria

- A unit aboard a fleet can be given a sea route with a cost and a month breakdown
- A crew without the sailing skill the ship requires is refused with that as the reason
- Land units are unaffected

## Notes

Two loose ends from #8 belong here. MovementMode has no Sail variant, deliberately. And
crates/core/src/movement/mode.rs has a can_swim function that nothing outside its own test calls -
this ruleset's water rule exempts only flight from needing a ship, so swimming currently decides
nothing; it should either be used here or deleted.

## Dependencies / Links

- Main issue: #1
- Out of scope of: #8

title: Import lots of reports
description:
There are plenty of old Borg reports that could be imported to the code base to potentially be used for testing. This issue should cover importing them into the code base in a structured way and they should be used by later issues.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The Borg reports are committed under a documented location in the repository.
- File naming encodes game, faction and turn so a test can select a report without opening it.
- A short document records where the reports came from and what they may be used for.
